summary: Specifies the messages of the Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6, used to report errors and carry diagnostic information. Tools such as ping depend on it. It was a draft standard, replaced by RFC 4443.

plainLanguage.summary: ICMPv6 is the control protocol built into IPv6. A node uses it to report that a packet could not be delivered or that a header was malformed, and to answer the echo requests that the ping utility sends. Every IPv6 node has to implement it.

questions: how does ping work in ipv6
what are the icmpv6 message types
what is the icmpv6 next header value
subtitle: The control messages that IPv6 nodes use to report errors and to test whether a host is reachable.

tldr.problem: IPv6 nodes need a way to tell a sender that a packet could not be delivered, that it was too big for the next link, that its hop limit ran out or that a header field was wrong.
tldr.mechanism: ICMPv6 defines four error message types and two informational types, each with a Type, a Code, a checksum and a body that carries as much of the offending packet as fits. The protocol number is 58 and the checksum covers a pseudo-header taken from the IPv6 header.
tldr.outcome: Every IPv6 node must implement ICMPv6, and the error messages feed Path MTU Discovery and the ping utility. The specification has been replaced by RFC 4443.

today: RFC 2463 was a Draft Standard published in December 1998. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4443, which is the current specification of ICMPv6.

sections.title: ICMPv6 and IPv6
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol version 6 is a new version of IP. IPv6 uses the Internet Control Message Protocol as defined for IPv4, with a number of changes. The resulting protocol is called ICMPv6, and it has an IPv6 Next Header value of 58, which is different from the value used to identify ICMP for IPv4.

ICMPv6 is used by IPv6 nodes to report errors encountered in processing packets, and to perform other internet-layer functions such as diagnostics. The RFC describes the format of the control messages used in ICMPv6, and it is an integral part of IPv6 that MUST be fully implemented by every IPv6 node.

The document does not describe the procedures for using these messages to achieve functions like Path MTU discovery, since those procedures are described in other documents. Other documents may also introduce additional ICMPv6 message types, such as Neighbor Discovery messages, subject to the general rules for ICMPv6 messages given in section 2 of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 needs a way to report problems with packets, so every IPv6 node speaks ICMPv6. It uses protocol number 58, which is different from the number used by the IPv4 version.

sections.title: The ICMPv6 Message Format
sections.content:
ICMPv6 messages are grouped into two classes. Error messages are identified as such by having a zero in the high-order bit of their message Type field values, so error messages have message Types from 0 to 127. Informational messages have message Types from 128 to 255.

The document defines four error messages: Type 1 Destination Unreachable, Type 2 Packet Too Big, Type 3 Time Exceeded and Type 4 Parameter Problem. It defines two informational messages: Type 128 Echo Request and Type 129 Echo Reply.

Every ICMPv6 message is preceded by an IPv6 header and zero or more IPv6 extension headers, and the ICMPv6 header is identified by a Next Header value of 58 in the immediately preceding header.

The message itself has three fixed fields followed by a variable body. The Type field indicates the type of the message, and its value determines the format of the remaining data. The Code field depends on the message type and is used to create an additional level of message granularity. The Checksum field detects data corruption in the ICMPv6 message and in parts of the IPv6 header.

The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the entire ICMPv6 message, starting with the message type field, prepended with a pseudo-header of IPv6 header fields. The Next Header value used in the pseudo-header is 58. Including a pseudo-header in the ICMPv6 checksum is a change from IPv4. For computing the checksum, the checksum field itself is set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Every ICMPv6 message starts with three fields: a type number, a code that gives the detail, and a checksum. Type numbers below 128 report errors, and numbers from 128 to 255 carry information such as the answer to a ping.

sections.title: Message Processing Rules
sections.content:
Implementations MUST observe a set of rules when processing ICMPv6 messages. If an error message of unknown type is received it MUST be passed to the upper layer, while an informational message of unknown type MUST be silently discarded. Every error message, that is, one with type less than 128, includes as much of the offending packet, the packet that caused the error, as will fit without making the error message packet exceed the minimum IPv6 MTU.

Where the internet-layer protocol is required to pass an error message to the upper-layer process, the upper-layer protocol type is extracted from the original packet contained in the body of the error message and used to select the appropriate upper-layer process. If the original packet had an unusually large amount of extension headers, the upper-layer protocol type may not be present in the error message because of truncation to meet the minimum IPv6 MTU limit, in which case the error message is silently dropped after any IPv6-layer processing.

An error message MUST NOT be sent as a result of receiving an ICMPv6 error message, a packet destined to an IPv6 multicast address, a packet sent as a link-layer multicast or broadcast, or a packet whose source address does not uniquely identify a single node. Two exceptions apply to the multicast cases: the Packet Too Big message is sent so that Path MTU discovery works for IPv6 multicast, and the Parameter Problem message with Code 2 reporting an unrecognized IPv6 option whose Option Type highest-order two bits are set to 10.

To limit the bandwidth and forwarding costs of sending error messages, an IPv6 node MUST limit the rate of ICMPv6 error messages it sends. This can happen when a source sending a stream of erroneous packets fails to heed the resulting error messages. Two kinds of limit are given as examples: a timer-based limit, for example limiting transmission of error messages to a given source, or to any source, to at most once every T milliseconds, and a bandwidth-based limit, for example limiting the rate of error messages sent from a particular interface to some fraction F of the attached link's bandwidth. The limit parameters MUST be configurable for the node, with a conservative default value, for example T equal to 1 second and not 0 seconds, or F equal to 2 percent and not 100 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: Nodes follow strict rules about when to send an error and how fast. Sending an error in response to another error is forbidden, and a node must slow down its error messages so that a flood of bad packets cannot flood the network back.

sections.title: The Four Error Messages
sections.content:
Destination Unreachable, Type 1, has an Unused field that must be initialized to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. Code 0 means no route to destination, Code 1 means communication with the destination administratively prohibited, Code 2 is not assigned, Code 3 means address unreachable and Code 4 means port unreachable. A Destination Unreachable message SHOULD be generated by a router, or by the IPv6 layer in the originating node, in response to a packet that cannot be delivered for reasons other than congestion, and it MUST NOT be generated if a packet is dropped due to congestion. A destination node SHOULD send one with Code 4 for a packet whose transport protocol, such as UDP, has no listener, if that transport protocol has no alternative way to inform the sender.

Packet Too Big, Type 2, has Code set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver, and an MTU field giving the Maximum Transmission Unit of the next-hop link. A router MUST send it when it cannot forward a packet because the packet is larger than the MTU of the outgoing link, and the information is used as part of the Path MTU Discovery process. Unlike other error messages it is sent in response to a packet received with an IPv6 multicast destination address, or a link-layer multicast or broadcast address.

Time Exceeded, Type 3, has Code 0 for hop limit exceeded in transit and Code 1 for fragment reassembly time exceeded. If a router receives a packet with a Hop Limit of zero, or decrements a packet's Hop Limit to zero, it MUST discard the packet and send a Time Exceeded message with Code 0 to the source. This indicates either a routing loop or too small an initial Hop Limit value.

Parameter Problem, Type 4, has a Pointer field that identifies the octet offset within the invoking packet where the error was detected. Code 0 means an erroneous header field was encountered, Code 1 an unrecognized Next Header type and Code 2 an unrecognized IPv6 option. If an IPv6 node finds a problem with a field in the IPv6 header or extension headers such that it cannot complete processing the packet, it MUST discard the packet and SHOULD send a Parameter Problem message indicating the type and location of the problem. A message with Type 4, Code 1 and Pointer 40 would indicate that the IPv6 extension header following the IPv6 header of the original packet holds an unrecognized Next Header field value.
sections.plainLanguage: The four error messages cover the four things that can go wrong: the packet cannot be delivered, it is too big for the next link, the hop limit ran out, or a header field was wrong. Each carries a code saying which case it is.

sections.title: Echo Request and Echo Reply
sections.content:
The Echo Request message, Type 128, has Code 0, an Identifier and a Sequence Number that aid in matching Echo Replies to the request and may each be zero, and zero or more octets of arbitrary Data. Every node MUST implement an ICMPv6 Echo responder function that receives Echo Requests and sends corresponding Echo Replies, and a node SHOULD also implement an application-layer interface for sending Echo Requests and receiving Echo Replies for diagnostic purposes. The Destination Address may be any legal IPv6 address.

The Echo Reply message, Type 129, has Code 0, and its Identifier, Sequence Number and Data are copied from the invoking Echo Request. The Destination Address is copied from the Source Address field of the invoking Echo Request packet.

The source address of an Echo Reply sent in response to a unicast Echo Request MUST be the same as the destination address of that Echo Request. An Echo Reply SHOULD be sent in response to an Echo Request sent to an IPv6 multicast address, and the source address of the reply MUST be a unicast address belonging to the interface on which the multicast Echo Request was received. The data received in the Echo Request MUST be returned entirely and unmodified in the Echo Reply. Echo Reply messages MUST be passed to the process that originated the Echo Request message, and may also be passed to processes that did not originate it.
sections.plainLanguage: An Echo Request carries an identifier, a sequence number and some data. The node that receives it sends back an Echo Reply carrying the same three, unchanged. That exchange is what the ping utility uses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ICMP protocol packet exchanges can be authenticated using the IP Authentication Header. A node SHOULD include an Authentication Header when sending ICMP messages if a security association for use with it exists for the destination address, and such associations may have been created through manual configuration or through a key management protocol. Received Authentication Headers in ICMP packets MUST be verified for correctness, and packets with incorrect authentication MUST be ignored and discarded. It SHOULD be possible for the system administrator to configure a node to ignore any ICMP messages that are not authenticated using either the Authentication Header or the Encapsulating Security Payload, and such a switch SHOULD default to allowing unauthenticated messages. Confidentiality issues are addressed by the IP Security Architecture and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload documents.

The RFC lists four attacks. ICMP messages may be subject to actions intended to make the receiver believe the message came from a different source than the message originator; the protection is to apply the IPv6 Authentication mechanism to the message. They may be subject to actions intended to make the message or its reply go to a destination other than the originator intended; the ICMP checksum protects the source and destination address of the packet carrying the message, provided the checksum field is itself protected by authentication or encryption. They may be subject to changes in the message fields or payload, and authentication or encryption protects against that. And they may be used as attempts to perform denial of service attacks by sending back to back erroneous IP packets, against which an implementation that correctly follows the rate limiting rules is protected.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can send an ICMPv6 message that claims to come from somewhere else, so the protocol offers a way to authenticate them. Nodes must also limit how fast they send error messages, which is what stops a flood of bad packets from turning into a denial of service.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The type of the message; its value determines the format of the remaining data.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Depends on the message type and adds a level of granularity.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Detects data corruption in the message and in parts of the IPv6 header.

viz.caption: THE ICMPv6 MESSAGE TYPES DEFINED HERE

items.label: Destination Unreachable
items.desc: The packet cannot be delivered; the code says why.

items.label: Packet Too Big
items.desc: The packet is larger than the MTU of the outgoing link.

items.label: Time Exceeded
items.desc: The hop limit ran out, or fragment reassembly took too long.

items.label: Parameter Problem
items.desc: A header field was wrong; the pointer gives the octet offset.

items.label: Echo Request
items.desc: A diagnostic request asking whether a node is reachable.

items.label: Echo Reply
items.desc: The answer to an Echo Request, carrying the same data back.

viz.caption: THE ECHO REQUEST AND ECHO REPLY EXCHANGE

messages.label: ECHO REQUEST (128)
messages.note: Carries an identifier, a sequence number and arbitrary data.

messages.label: ECHO REPLY (129)
messages.note: Returns the identifier, sequence number and data unchanged.
